title: Three Prescriptions for Thinking More Clearly about Teaching, Part 1: Consume Fewer Urgent Things onsumption-of-the-urgent/
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. opens a three-part series on clear thinking as a foundation for teacher flourishing, and this first part prescribes severely limiting consumption of the urgent. His reasoning borrows from how we coach students: quantity precedes quality, so if we want more thinking we must clear room for sustained thought. He singles out social media, email and the news as the usual culprits, describing his own fixes of removing apps and email from his phone and setting browser time limits. He reports that his email responses actually improved once he stopped checking constantly. He frames the choice as rejecting an 'any-benefit' approach to decisions, since good things can still crowd out the best, and tells readers to redirect the reclaimed time to reading something costly or to writing.
points: Clear thinking is an earned skill that depends on protected time for sustained thought, so the first move is subtraction rather than addition.
Social media, email and news are singled out because they reward speed and constant checking, which erodes the mental space needed to reflect.
Removing apps and email from his phone improved rather than harmed his response times, evidence that constraint can sharpen work.
The 'any-benefit' trap means an activity being useful is not enough; a teacher has to ask whether it is the optimal use of limited attention.
quotes: Lots of promises there, right? But thinking clearly, especially in our time, is hard. It's an earned skill, not a spur of the moment decision.
If you'd like students to get better at reading or writing or speaking or designing experiments, what should you have them do? Read, write, speak, or design experiments. Quantity precedes quality.

But there is only so much time! To go back to our students, we make more room for more reading and writing and speaking by eliminating fluff and inefficiencies. For us, we've got to eliminate activities in our days that pull us away from sustained thought.
As Robert Greene writes in Laws of Human Nature, “[Social media] are not media designed for calm reflection. With their constant presence, we have less and less mental space to step back and think.
For the past year, I've not been able to do that because I don't have email there. And, guess what? My response times haven't gotten worse — they've not even stayed the same. They've improved.
The business model of news is that there are urgent things you need to know right now. But this week's breaking news is rarely next month's important story.
